name: Availability Attribute
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Up and Reachable: Availability as a Quality Attribute in Blockchain Systems
lesson.summary: Availability measures the fraction of time a system is operational and able to service requests, and blockchains pursue it through redundancy across many independent nodes rather than through any single highly reliable machine.
lesson.body:
Availability is the quality attribute concerned with whether a system is up and able to respond when a request arrives, typically expressed as a percentage of time over some period, often described informally in nines: ninety nine point nine percent availability allows roughly nine hours of downtime a year, ninety nine point nine nine percent allows roughly under an hour. Availability is closely related to, but distinct from, reliability: reliability asks whether the system produces a correct response when it does respond, while availability asks only whether a response, correct or not, arrives at all. A system can be highly available and still wrong, or briefly unavailable and, once it comes back, entirely correct.

Traditional systems pursue availability through redundant hardware, failover servers, and geographically distributed data centers, all controlled by one organization that decides how much redundancy is worth paying for. Blockchains pursue availability differently: instead of one organization operating several redundant servers, thousands of independently operated nodes each hold a full copy of the ledger, so the failure or shutdown of any single node, or any modest number of nodes, does not affect whether the network as a whole keeps producing blocks and answering queries. This is the availability payoff of the decentralization the earlier fork and governance chapters described: no single operator's outage is the network's outage.

That payoff depends on the number and independence of nodes actually staying high, and it can fail in practice even in systems marketed as highly available. Solana, a proof of stake blockchain optimized heavily for throughput, has experienced multiple network wide outages since 2021, including incidents where validator software bugs or resource exhaustion under heavy transaction load halted block production entirely for extended periods until node operators coordinated a manual restart. These outages are a direct, observable availability failure: for the duration of the halt, the network could not process a single transaction for anyone, regardless of how many validators nominally existed, because the failure mode was shared across nearly all of them at once rather than isolated to a few.

The Solana outages illustrate a subtlety availability analysis has to catch: redundancy only protects availability against failures that are independent across nodes. If every node runs the same client software and hits the same bug under the same load pattern, having ten thousand nodes provides no more availability than having one, because they all fail together. A quality attribute scenario for availability written honestly for such a network would include client diversity, whether multiple independently maintained implementations of the protocol exist, as part of the environment, since a monoculture of one client is a sensitivity point for availability even in a heavily decentralized network.

For a skeptic evaluating a blockchain's availability claims, the useful question is rarely how many nodes exist, but how correlated their failure modes are: shared client software, shared cloud hosting provider, shared geographic region, or shared dependence on one centralized service all quietly convert a nominally decentralized, highly available architecture back into something with a single point of failure in disguise.
